title: Foundations of Strategic Thinking
short: Players, strategies, payoffs, and the logic of dominance.

outcomes.text: Define the elements of a strategic game: players, strategies, payoffs and information.
Identify strictly dominant and dominated strategies and apply iterated elimination.
Construct a payoff matrix that models a real decision with interdependent payoffs.

lessons.title: What makes a situation a game
lessons.html:
A situation is a game when the outcome for each decision-maker depends on the choices of others. Two canteens setting prices, two clubs picking event dates and two bidders in an auction are all games; choosing an umbrella because of the weather forecast is not, because the weather does not respond to you.

Every game has four elements:

  • Players – the decision-makers.
  • Strategies – a complete plan of action, specifying what a player does in every situation they might face.
  • Payoffs – a number for each outcome, representing how much each player values it.
  • Information – what each player knows when they choose.

lessons.title: Normal form and the payoff matrix
lessons.html:
A simultaneous two-player game is written as a payoff matrix. Rows are Player 1's strategies, columns are Player 2's, and each cell lists (row payoff, column payoff).

Cooperate Defect
Cooperate (3, 3) (0, 5)
Defect (5, 0) (1, 1)

This is the Prisoner's Dilemma, the most studied game in social science. Read it from each player's point of view: if the other cooperates, you get 3 by cooperating and 5 by defecting; if they defect, you get 0 or 1.

lessons.title: Dominance and iterated elimination
lessons.html:
A strategy is strictly dominant if it gives a strictly higher payoff than every alternative, whatever the opponents do. In the matrix above, Defect is strictly dominant for both players, so rational players reach (Defect, Defect) and earn 1 each, although both prefer (Cooperate, Cooperate). That gap between individual and collective rationality is the dilemma.

When no strategy is dominant, remove strategies that are strictly dominated, then look again: removing one player's bad options can create dominance for the other. This is iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS).

questions.prompt: Define: in game theory, a strategy is best described as…
options: A complete plan of action that specifies a choice in every situation the player might face
The payoff a player receives at the end of the game
The outcome that maximises total welfare
The probability that the opponent cooperates
questions.explanation: A strategy is a complete contingent plan; payoffs and outcomes are consequences of strategy profiles.

questions.prompt: Explain why Defect is a strictly dominant strategy in the one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma (T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0).
options: It gives a strictly higher payoff whatever the other player does (5>3 and 1>0)
It maximises the sum of both players' payoffs
The other player is known to defect
It is the only strategy that forms a Pareto-optimal outcome
questions.explanation: Compare column by column: against Cooperate, 5 > 3; against Defect, 1 > 0. Defect wins in every case.

questions.prompt: Compute the IESDS outcome. Payoffs (Row, Col): (U,L)=(3,1), (U,R)=(0,2), (D,L)=(2,3), (D,R)=(1,4).
options: (U, L)
(U, R)
(D, L)
(D, R)
questions.explanation: For Column, R beats L in both rows (2>1, 4>3), so L is eliminated. Facing R, Row prefers D (1>0). Outcome (D,R) = (1,4).

questions.prompt: Analyze: two campus canteens each choose a thali price. Which feature makes this a game rather than a single-person decision?
options: Each canteen's profit depends on the other canteen's price
Both canteens want to maximise profit
Prices are numbers
Students prefer cheaper food
questions.explanation: Strategic interdependence – your payoff depends on another decision-maker's choice – is what defines a game.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the claim: “If every player is rational, the group always reaches the best collective outcome.”
options: False – in the Prisoner's Dilemma individually rational play gives (D,D), which both players rank below (C,C)
True – rational players always coordinate on the Pareto-optimal outcome
True, but only in zero-sum games
It cannot be evaluated without knowing the players' names
questions.explanation: The PD is the classic counter-example: dominance reasoning leads to an outcome that is Pareto-dominated.

questions.prompt: Design a 2×2 payoff matrix for a real campus situation (for example, two clubs choosing whether to schedule their fest on the same weekend) in which each player has a strictly dominant strategy. Label players, strategies and payoffs, and state the predicted outcome.
rubric: Two named players and two named strategies each
Payoffs written for every cell as (row, column)
A strictly dominant strategy shown for each player by explicit comparison
Predicted outcome stated, with a comment on whether it is Pareto-optimal
questions.model: Clubs A and B choose Same weekend / Different weekend. Payoffs: (S,S)=(2,2), (S,D)=(5,1), (D,S)=(1,5), (D,D)=(4,4). S strictly dominates for both: against S, 2>1; against D, 5>4. Prediction (S,S) with (2,2), Pareto-dominated by (D,D) – a dilemma.

title: Nash Equilibrium
short: Best responses, pure and mixed equilibria, and coordination problems.

outcomes.text: Define best response and Nash equilibrium.
Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of a matrix game by marking best responses.
Compute mixed-strategy equilibria of 2×2 games using the indifference principle.

lessons.title: Best responses
lessons.html: A best response is the strategy that maximises your payoff given what the others do. To find them in a matrix, go column by column and underline Row's highest payoff; then go row by row and underline Column's highest payoff.

lessons.title: Nash equilibrium
lessons.html:
A Nash equilibrium is a profile of strategies in which every player is playing a best response to the others. Equivalently: no player can gain by changing their strategy alone. In the matrix, it is any cell where both payoffs are underlined.

Games can have one equilibrium (Prisoner's Dilemma), several (Stag Hunt, Battle of the Sexes, Chicken) or none in pure strategies (Matching Pennies).

lessons.title: Mixed strategies and indifference
lessons.html:
When no pure equilibrium exists, players randomise. In a mixed equilibrium each player mixes so that the opponent is indifferent between their own pure strategies – otherwise the opponent would pick one and the mix would not be stable.

Row plays U with prob p. Column indifferent when:
p·u₂(U,L) + (1−p)·u₂(D,L) = p·u₂(U,R) + (1−p)·u₂(D,R)

Notice that Row's probability is pinned down by Column's payoffs. Nash's 1950 theorem guarantees that every finite game has at least one equilibrium once mixing is allowed.

lessons.title: Multiple equilibria and selection
lessons.html: In the Stag Hunt, (Stag, Stag) gives both players the most, so it is payoff-dominant. (Hare, Hare) is safer: it is risk-dominant because deviating from it costs more if the other player is uncertain. Which equilibrium a group reaches depends on trust, history and communication. Use the Nash Solver in the Arena to test this on your own matrices.

questions.prompt: Define: a Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile in which…
options: No player can increase their payoff by unilaterally changing strategy
The total payoff of all players is maximised
Every player uses a dominant strategy
Players have agreed to cooperate
questions.explanation: Mutual best responses – no profitable unilateral deviation.

questions.prompt: Explain why Matching Pennies has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
options: In every cell one of the two players would gain by switching
Both players have a dominant strategy
The payoffs sum to zero, which rules out equilibria
Players move sequentially
questions.explanation: The matcher wants to match and the mismatcher wants to mismatch, so every cell has a profitable deviation for someone.

questions.prompt: Compute: Column's payoffs are (U,L)=4, (U,R)=1, (D,L)=0, (D,R)=2. In the mixed equilibrium Row plays U with probability p that makes Column indifferent. p = ?
Analyze the Stag Hunt: (S,S)=(4,4), (S,H)=(0,3), (H,S)=(3,0), (H,H)=(3,3). Which are the pure Nash equilibria?
options: (Stag, Stag) and (Hare, Hare)
Only (Stag, Stag)
Only (Hare, Hare)
(Stag, Hare) and (Hare, Stag)
questions.explanation: At (S,S) deviating gives 3<4; at (H,H) deviating gives 0<3. Off-diagonal cells have a profitable deviation.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: which judgement about the two Stag Hunt equilibria is best justified?
options: (Stag,Stag) is payoff-dominant but (Hare,Hare) is risk-dominant, so the outcome depends on players' beliefs about each other
(Stag,Stag) will always be played because it pays more
(Hare,Hare) is not really an equilibrium
Both are equally likely in every population
questions.explanation: Risk dominance compares deviation losses: (3−0)(3−0)=9 at (H,H) vs (4−3)(4−3)=1 at (S,S). Trust decides.

questions.prompt: Design a 2×2 game that has no pure-strategy equilibrium and exactly one mixed equilibrium. Give the matrix and compute both players' equilibrium mixing probabilities.
rubric: Matrix in which every cell has a profitable unilateral deviation
Indifference equation written for each player
Both probabilities computed correctly and lie strictly between 0 and 1
Check: verify with the Arena's Nash Solver
questions.model: Penalty kick: Kicker (Left/Right) vs Keeper (Left/Right). Kicker payoff (scoring prob ×10): (L,L)=4, (L,R)=9, (R,L)=8, (R,R)=3; Keeper gets 10 minus that. Keeper dives L with q: 4q+9(1−q)=8q+3(1−q) → q=0.6. Kicker kicks L with p: keeper indifferent → 6p+2(1−p)=1p+7(1−p) → p=0.5.

title: Repeated Games & the Evolution of Cooperation
short: The shadow of the future, Tit-for-Tat and Axelrod's tournaments.

outcomes.text: Describe the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma and the role of the discount factor δ.
Explain how trigger strategies sustain cooperation and derive the critical δ.
Evaluate strategies' performance in round-robin and noisy tournaments.

lessons.title: The shadow of the future
lessons.html:
Play the Prisoner's Dilemma once and defection dominates. Play it again and again with an uncertain end and things change: today's defection can be punished tomorrow. Model this with a continuation probability (or discount factor) δ – the chance the game continues to another round.

If the number of rounds is known and finite, backward induction unravels cooperation: everyone defects in the last round, so the second-last round is effectively the last, and so on back to round one.

lessons.title: Trigger strategies
lessons.html:
Grim Trigger cooperates until the opponent defects once, then defects forever. Cooperation is an equilibrium when the gain from cheating today is smaller than the future loss:

R/(1−δ) ≥ T + δ·P/(1−δ) ⇔ δ ≥ (T − R)/(T − P)

With the club's standard payoffs T=5, R=3, P=1 the threshold is δ ≥ 0.5: if each round has at least a 50% chance of being followed by another, cooperation can be self-enforcing.

lessons.title: Axelrod's tournaments
lessons.html:
In 1980 Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit strategies for a round-robin repeated PD. The simplest entry, Tit-for-Tat (cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move), won both tournaments. Axelrod identified four properties of successful strategies:

  • Nice – never the first to defect.
  • Retaliatory – punish defection promptly.
  • Forgiving – return to cooperation after punishment.
  • Clear – easy for others to recognise and adapt to.

lessons.title: Noise and robustness
lessons.html: With implementation errors, two TFT players can fall into an endless echo of retaliation after a single mistake. Generous TFT (forgive some defections) and Pavlov / Win-Stay-Lose-Shift recover from errors faster. Run the Arena's tournament with noise switched on and watch the ranking change.

questions.prompt: Recall: Tit-for-Tat plays…
options: Cooperate in round 1, then whatever the opponent did in the previous round
Defect in round 1, then copy the opponent
Cooperate until the opponent defects, then defect forever
Randomly with probability 0.5
questions.explanation: That is the definition; the third option is Grim Trigger.

questions.prompt: Explain why cooperation can survive in an indefinitely repeated PD but not in one with a known final round.
options: With a known end, backward induction makes every round a one-shot game; with an uncertain end, future punishment remains a credible threat
Players become friends over time
Payoffs increase in later rounds
The dominant strategy changes after round 10
questions.explanation: Unravelling requires a known last round. Uncertainty keeps the shadow of the future alive.

questions.prompt: Compute: with T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0, Grim Trigger sustains cooperation if and only if δ ≥ …
Analyze: two Tit-for-Tat players meet in a noisy match where one cooperation is accidentally flipped to defection. What follows?
options: An alternating echo (C/D, D/C, …) of retaliation until another error breaks it
Immediate return to mutual cooperation
Permanent mutual defection, like Grim Trigger
Nothing changes because TFT ignores single defections
questions.explanation: Each TFT copies the other's last move, so the single defection bounces back and forth.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: TFT never scores more than its opponent in any single match, yet it won Axelrod's tournament. The best explanation is…
options: Total score comes from eliciting mutual cooperation with many partners; beating individual opponents is not the objective
The tournament rules favoured simple strategies
TFT was lucky in the random draws
Other strategies were not rational
questions.explanation: Payoffs are absolute, not relative. A strategy that creates many (3,3) rounds accumulates more than one that wins small head-to-head contests.

questions.prompt: Design your own repeated-PD strategy that is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and robust to 5% noise. Write its rules precisely, then predict (and test in the Arena tournament) how it performs against TFT and Always Defect.
rubric: Rules specify the move for every possible history (complete strategy)
Each of Axelrod's four properties is demonstrated
A mechanism to escape noise-induced echoes
Prediction stated, then compared with tournament results
questions.model: “Contrite Generous TFT”: cooperate first; if the opponent defected last round, defect with probability 0.9 (forgive 10%); if my own last defection was an accident, accept one punishment without retaliating. Against TFT: near-full cooperation; against ALLD: loses ≈ 0.1×S per round versus pure TFT.

title: Probability, Expected Value & the House Edge
short: Why the wheel always wins: EV, the law of large numbers and betting systems.

outcomes.text: Compute the expected value of a bet.
Explain the house edge and the law of large numbers.
Analyze betting systems such as Martingale and the risk of ruin.

lessons.title: Expected value
lessons.html:
The expected value of a bet is the probability-weighted average of its outcomes: EV = Σ pᵢ·xᵢ. A European roulette wheel has 37 pockets: 1–36 and a single green 0.

Straight-up (pays 35:1): EV = (1/37)(+35) + (36/37)(−1) = −1/37 ≈ −2.70%
Red (pays 1:1): EV = (18/37)(+1) + (19/37)(−1) = −1/37 ≈ −2.70%

Every standard bet has the same edge, because payouts are set as if the wheel had 36 pockets. The zero is the house's margin. American wheels add a 00, doubling the edge to 2/38 ≈ 5.26%.

lessons.title: The law of large numbers
lessons.html: Over a few spins anything can happen. Over thousands, the average result per unit staked converges to the EV. A player can win tonight; a casino with millions of spins cannot lose. In the Arena's roulette table, the dashed line on the bankroll chart is the EV path – watch your real bankroll wander around it and drift down.

lessons.title: Betting systems and ruin
lessons.html: Martingale doubles the stake after each loss so that the first win recovers everything plus one unit. It wins small amounts often and loses a very large amount rarely: after 10 straight losses on red (probability ≈ (19/37)¹⁰ ≈ 0.13%) the next stake is 1,024 units. Table limits and finite bankrolls make that collapse certain over enough play. No staking pattern changes the EV of the individual bets; it only reshapes the distribution of outcomes.

questions.prompt: Recall: how many pockets does a European roulette wheel have?
questions.explanation: 1–36 plus a single zero.

questions.prompt: Explain why every standard bet on a European wheel has the same house edge of 1/37.
options: Payouts are set as if there were 36 pockets, so the extra zero pocket is the house's margin on every bet
Because red and black are equally likely
Because the casino adjusts the wheel
Because bets on single numbers pay more
questions.explanation: Fair odds on 36 pockets; the 37th pocket turns them unfair by exactly 1/37.

questions.prompt: Compute the EV of a ₹100 bet on a dozen (12 numbers, pays 2:1) on a European wheel.
Analyze why the Martingale system fails over the long run.
options: It trades many small wins for rare catastrophic losses; finite bankrolls and table limits stop the doubling, and each bet's EV stays negative
It works, but casinos ban it
It fails only on American wheels
It fails because spins are not independent
questions.explanation: Staking cannot change EV; it concentrates losses into rare, large ruin events.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: a friend won five roulette sessions in a row and says their system “beats the wheel”. The best assessment is…
options: Five wins are consistent with a negative-EV game; spins are independent and a small sample says little about the long-run average
The system must work; five wins is unlikely by chance
They should double their stakes
Roulette is a game of skill, so it is plausible
questions.explanation: Short streaks are common under negative EV. Only large samples reveal the edge.

questions.prompt: Design a simulation experiment, using the Arena's Strategy Lab, comparing flat betting with Martingale. State your hypothesis, the parameters (players, spins, bankroll, base stake) and the metrics you will report.
rubric: Clear, falsifiable hypothesis
Parameters fixed and justified (e.g., 1,000 players × 100 spins, ₹1,000 bankroll, ₹10 base)
Metrics include mean and median final bankroll and ruin rate
Interpretation linking results to EV and variance
questions.model: H: both systems lose ≈2.7% of total stake on average, but Martingale has a higher median and a far higher ruin rate. Run 1,000 players × 100 spins, ₹1,000 bankroll, ₹10 base stake on red; report mean/median final bankroll, % ruined, max drawdown.

title: Auctions & Mechanism Design
short: First- vs second-price, truthful bidding and the winner's curse.

outcomes.text: Explain why truthful bidding is weakly dominant in a Vickrey auction.
Analyze bid shading, revenue equivalence and the winner's curse.

lessons.title: Four standard formats
lessons.html:
• English – ascending open outcry; the last bidder standing wins.
  • Dutch – the price falls until someone accepts.
  • First-price sealed bid – highest bid wins and pays its own bid.
  • Second-price sealed bid (Vickrey) – highest bid wins and pays the second-highest bid.

lessons.title: Why truth-telling works in Vickrey auctions
lessons.html: In a second-price auction your bid decides only whether you win, never the price you pay. Bidding above your value can make you win when the second bid exceeds your value (a loss); bidding below can make you lose an auction you would have won profitably. Bidding exactly your value is therefore weakly dominant. William Vickrey received the 1996 Nobel Prize partly for this insight.

lessons.title: Bid shading and revenue equivalence
lessons.html:
In a first-price auction you must shade your bid below your value to make any profit. With n bidders whose values are independent and uniform, the symmetric equilibrium bid is:

b(v) = ((n − 1)/n) · v

The revenue equivalence theorem says that, with risk-neutral bidders and independent private values, all four formats give the seller the same expected revenue. Break an assumption – risk-averse bidders, correlated values, asymmetric bidders – and the formats diverge.

lessons.title: The winner's curse
lessons.html: When the item has a common value that everyone estimates with error (an oil field, a spectrum licence), the winner is the bidder with the most optimistic estimate. Winning is itself bad news about your estimate. Rational bidders shade their bids to account for it.

questions.prompt: Recall: in a sealed-bid second-price (Vickrey) auction the winner pays…
options: The second-highest bid
Their own bid
The average bid
The reserve price only
questions.explanation: That is the defining rule.

questions.prompt: Explain why bidding your true value is weakly dominant in a Vickrey auction.
options: Your bid only decides whether you win, not the price; overbidding risks paying more than your value and underbidding risks losing profitable wins
Because others will bid truthfully too
Because the seller requires it
Because it maximises the seller's revenue
questions.explanation: Price is set by others' bids, so the only effect of your bid is the win/lose boundary – put it at your value.

questions.prompt: Compute: first-price auction, 4 bidders, values i.i.d. uniform on [0, 100]. Your value is 80. What is the symmetric equilibrium bid?
Analyze: which broken assumption makes a first-price auction raise more expected revenue than a second-price auction?
options: Bidders are risk-averse
Bidders are risk-neutral
Values are independent
Bidders are symmetric
questions.explanation: Risk-averse bidders shade less in first-price auctions to avoid losing, raising revenue; second-price bidding is unaffected.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: winners of common-value auctions (e.g., oil leases) often lose money. The best explanation is…
options: The winner's curse – winning means your estimate was the most optimistic, so unshaded bids overpay on average
Sellers manipulate the auctions
Bidders always bid irrationally
Second-price rules are unfair
questions.explanation: Conditioning on winning reveals your estimate was high; failing to correct for it causes systematic overpayment.

questions.prompt: Design an auction that allocates 3 expert-mentoring slots among 20 hackathon teams using club credits, so that bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy. Specify the rules, the price paid and how ties are broken.
rubric: Sealed bids in credits with clear eligibility
Uniform price set by the highest losing bid (4th-highest), or a VCG argument
Explains why truthful bidding is dominant
Tie-breaking and budget rules stated
questions.model: Sealed bids; top 3 bids win; each winner pays the 4th-highest bid (uniform (k+1)-th price). With unit demand, a team's bid affects only whether it wins, so bidding its value is dominant. Ties broken by earlier submission time; bids cannot exceed credit balance.

title: Bargaining, Fairness & Bounded Rationality
short: Ultimatum offers, level-k thinking and the Keynesian beauty contest.

outcomes.text: Describe the ultimatum game and its subgame-perfect equilibrium.
Explain experimental deviations from equilibrium using fairness preferences.
Apply level-k reasoning to the guess-2/3-of-the-average game.

lessons.title: The ultimatum game
lessons.html:
A proposer offers a split of ₹100; the responder accepts (both get the split) or rejects (both get nothing). By backward induction the responder accepts any positive amount, so the subgame-perfect equilibrium is the smallest positive offer, accepted.

Experiments across many countries show something else: modal offers are 40–50%, and offers below about 20% are rejected roughly half the time. Responders pay to punish unfairness, and proposers anticipate it.

lessons.title: Level-k thinking
lessons.html:
In guess 2/3 of the average, everyone picks 0–100 and the closest to two-thirds of the average wins. Iterated reasoning leads to the unique equilibrium, 0. Real players reason only a few steps:

Level-0: random, average 50
Level-1: 2/3 × 50 = 33.3
Level-2: 2/3 × 33.3 = 22.2
Level-3: 2/3 × 22.2 = 14.8 … Nash: 0

Winning numbers in classrooms and newspapers usually fall between 15 and 35. The best guess is a best response to the people actually playing, not to perfectly rational opponents. Keynes used the same idea to describe stock markets.

questions.prompt: Recall: in the subgame-perfect equilibrium of the ultimatum game (₹100, ₹1 units), the proposer offers…
options: ₹1, the smallest positive amount
Whatever the responder demands
questions.explanation: The responder prefers ₹1 to ₹0, so the proposer keeps ₹99.

questions.prompt: Explain why many responders reject offers of 10–20%.
options: They have preferences for fairness and are willing to give up money to punish unfair proposers
They cannot calculate payoffs
Rejection gives them more money
The rules reward rejection
questions.explanation: Inequity aversion and reciprocity models explain costly punishment.

questions.prompt: Compute: in a guess-2/3-of-the-average game, a level-2 thinker who believes level-0 players average 50 guesses about…
questions.explanation: Level-1 = 33.3; level-2 best-responds to level-1: 2/3 × 33.3 ≈ 22.2.

questions.prompt: Analyze: classroom winning numbers are usually 20–35, not the equilibrium 0. Why?
options: Most players reason only one or two steps, and the winning guess is a best response to the actual population
Players do not understand the rules
Random noise always pushes guesses up
The equilibrium is actually 33
questions.explanation: Bounded depth of reasoning shifts the average; the target follows the population, not theory.

questions.prompt: Evaluate: as proposer with ₹100, acceptance rates are 30% for offer 10, 60% for 30, 95% for 40 and 100% for 50. Which offer maximises your expected payoff?
Design a classroom experiment testing whether anonymity changes ultimatum-game offers. Specify treatment and control, participants, procedure, the measure and your prediction.
rubric: Control (names visible) and treatment (anonymous) clearly defined
Random assignment and adequate sample
Outcome measures: mean offer, rejection rate
Prediction grounded in fairness/reputation theory, plus a threat to validity
questions.model: Randomly assign 60 students to Visible or Anonymous pairing, ₹100 virtual stakes, one shot. Measure mean offer and rejection rate. Predict lower offers when anonymous (reputation concern removed). Threat: students discussing the game between sessions.
